subject: TTFT & streaming cadence - follow-up and SLO clarification
messages:
From: Aditya Rao <aditya@redwood.com>
To: Priya Singh <priya@acme.ai>, Tom Blake <tom.blake@acme.ai>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben@redwood.com>
Date: 2028-04-10T09:15:00-07:00
Subject: Follow-up: TTFT targets + streaming cadence (recap & asks)

Hi Priya / Tom —

Thanks again for the quick discovery call this morning. Wanted to capture the key items we discussed and a few asks so we can scope a short perf/validation run. High level: Acme wants a low time-to-first-token (TTFT) for interactive experiences plus reliable streaming chunk cadence for longer assistant responses.

Recap of requirements you called out:
- TTFT target: tight interactive requirement (goal: p95 <= 150ms; we discussed p99 tolerance)
- Streaming: SSE preferred (browser clients), chunk cadence ~100–150ms ideal; some longer responses can tolerate larger gaps
- Concurrency/throughput: typical concurrent users ~250, peak ~700, expected sustained concurrency ~300; tokens/sec (aggregate) ~12k at peak
- Sequence lengths: most requests are short (prompt ~40–120 tokens), responses average 80–400 tokens

Asks / next steps for us to validate feasibility:
1) Can you share a small set of representative request payloads (sample prompts + expected response sizes)? If you can upload to the Drive link we discussed or attach, that’s perfect (we can also take a sanitized dump).
2) Confirm whether the client must receive chunks every <=150ms for UX smoothness, or whether 150–250ms is acceptable for some flows.
3) Any firm SLO language you need (p95/p99) for TTFT, or should we propose specific numbers after an initial benchmark?

What I’ll do on our side:
- Run a focused TTFT/streaming test against a Dedicated instance (short smoke + configurable concurrency) using both SSE and WebSocket streaming to compare chunk cadence and TTFT.
- Attach: TTFT_benchmarks_v1.pdf (sample baseline numbers) and streaming_cadence_notes.xlsx (notes on chunk cadence and measurement approach).

If that works, I’ll loop in Marissa (perf lead) and Ben (solutions eng) to propose a 60-minute validation slot next week.

Thanks —
Aditya Rao
Account Exec, Redwood Inference
aditya@redwood.com
(Attachment: TTFT_benchmarks_v1.pdf; streaming_cadence_notes.xlsx)

From: Priya Singh <priya@acme.ai>
To: Aditya Rao <aditya@redwood.com>
Cc: Tom Blake <tom.blake@acme.ai>
Date: 2028-04-10T10:05:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Follow-up: TTFT targets + streaming cadence (recap & asks)

Hi Aditya —

Thanks for the write-up, that matches our priorities. Quick clarifications / answers below:

1) TTFT SLOs: Our immediate ask is interactive UX: p95 TTFT <= 150ms; p99 ideally <= 300ms. If you think p99 <= 300ms is a hard constraint, flag it — we can be flexible on p99 for now if you can hit p95 reliably.

2) Streaming cadence: For primary UI (web chat), we want perceived typing to be smooth. Target chunk cadence ~100–150ms is ideal. We can accept occasional gaps up to ~250ms for long backfills, but bursts >300ms are noticeable and reduce UX quality. So please treat 100–150ms as the cadence target.

3) Concurrency / throughput: Typical concurrent users ~250; sustained during business hours ~300; peak concurrent sessions up to ~700 during promos. Aggregate tokens/sec at peak ~12k (most responses are 80–400 tokens).

4) Payloads: I uploaded a small set of representative payloads to the Drive link you provided and attached a sanitized JSON too (acme_sample_payloads.json). The sample includes short prompts (~50 tokens) and longer generator prompts (~300 tokens) so you can test both fast TTFT and sustained streaming.

5) Protocol: SSE for browser is preferred (we use an event-source wrapper). WebSocket is OK if you can demonstrate lower jitter/control over chunk sizes, but SSE is what our front-end team will implement first.

SLO language: We don’t need contractual wording yet — this is a validation to make sure you can hit the interactive bar. After the validation we’ll discuss contractual SLOs.

Available for a perf validation slot next week on Tue/Wed afternoon PT.

Thanks,
Priya
Head of Product, Acme AI
priya@acme.ai
(Attachment: acme_sample_payloads.json)

Marissa / Ben — forwarding Priya’s reply and samples. Key asks: p95 TTFT <=150ms (goal), p99 <=300ms desirable; streaming cadence target 100–150ms (SSE preferred); concurrency up to 700 peak; tokens/sec ~12k at peak.

Can you advise feasibility and propose a short test plan? My suggested approach:
- Step 0: Sanity check on model variant & quantization we should use for low TTFT (Marissa)
- Step 1: Run a 2-hour smoke with synthetic concurrency ramp (50 → 300 → 700) using acme_sample_payloads.json to measure p50/p95/p99 TTFT and chunk cadence (SSE)
- Step 2: Run a per-chunk jitter analysis and compare SSE vs WebSocket streaming for chunk control
- Step 3: Share results and propose any config changes (batching, KV cache settings, autoscale knobs)

Can you also flag any gotchas (e.g., batching effects on TTFT, warm vs cold model cost, necessary instance size) so I can set customer expectations?

Priya is available Tue/Wed afternoon PT for a 60-min validation; if you can propose a slot I’ll lock it.

Thanks —
Aditya

From: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>
To: Aditya Rao <aditya@redwood.com>, Ben Carter <ben@redwood.com>, Priya Singh <priya@acme.ai>
Date: 2028-04-12T11:02:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Fw: Follow-up: TTFT targets + streaming cadence — need perf plan

Thanks Aditya — quick read and initial plan below. Short answer: feasible, but requires focused config and a small set of trade-offs.

Initial notes / recommendations:
- TTFT drivers: kernel latency (model size & quantization), request batching, KV cache warmness, and network hops. For interactive p95 <=150ms we typically recommend: smaller model variant if quality allows OR int8 quantized larger model on high-frequency NVLink instance; disable cross-request batching for latency-critical endpoints and use single-request fast-path where possible.

- Targets we’ll validate in the test: p50/p95/p99 TTFT (ms) and chunk cadence median/jitter. Aim to demonstrate p95 <=150ms and p99 <=300ms on the sample payloads. If hits p95 but p99 is higher, we’ll show how caching + pinning a hot model replica reduces tail.

Proposed test config (what we’ll run):
1) Model: m-compact-v1 (fast) and m-large-int8 (quantized)
2) Instance: dedicated GPU pool (4x A100-style instances) with local KV cache enabled
3) Batching: off for TTFT-critical route; optional micro-batching for throughput runs
4) Streaming: measure SSE event emission times; also run a WebSocket test to compare chunk jitter and control
5) Metrics: TTFT p50/p95/p99, chunk cadence median/std/jitter, tokens/sec, CPU/GPU utilization.

Timeline & next steps:
- I’ll draft a 90-min test plan and run the smoke tomorrow morning PT (will use acme_sample_payloads.json).
- Deliverable: perf report + recommended config + reproducible test script (we’ll include measurement harness).
- Schedule: Tue 2028-04-17 14:00 PT works for an initial review (Priya, please confirm).

Gotchas to call out for the customer:
- If the client is using a browser EventSource with a small chunk buffer on the front end, the perceived cadence is mostly driven by server-side chunking (we’ll measure server emit times).
- Network jitter on the client path can add variability — we’ll include a jitter analysis but recommend testing from a representative client region.
- Batching increases throughput but can add 40–200ms to TTFT depending on batch window. For strict TTFT SLOs we recommend per-request fast-paths.

Attachment: test-plan.md (outline + commands) — I’ll share the full script in the drive link.

Marissa Cole
Perf Lead, Redwood Inference
marissa@redwood.com
(Attachment: test-plan.md)
